newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Indian groups say Brazil land ruling "disastrous".
newsitem.headline: Indian groups say Brazil land ruling "disastrous".

text.p: A controversial ruling by the Brazilian government that five towns may remain inside a disputed Indian reservation sets a "disastrous" precedent for the future of Indian land, activists said on Thursday.

"Rather than revising the rules for the demarcation of Indian land, the government has privileged ranchers and gold miners at the expense of Indians," said Stephan Schwartzman, an anthropologist with the U.S.-based Environmental Defence Fund.

In a ruling considered a test of Brazil's new approach to Indian land rights, the Justice Ministry on Monday announced that 50 farms in the vast Raposa/Serra do Sol reservation were illegal and would have to move. But it said five towns in the reservation in the northernmost state of Roraima may continue to exist and the reservation's as yet unmarked perimeter must skirt several farms awarded to settlers by the government.

The case of Raposa/Serra do Sol was considered the most sensitive of dozens of challenges to the demarcation of Indian lands brought by landowners and local governments. Indian groups said the ruling meant 494,000 acres (200,000 hectares) would be lost from the 4 million-acre (1.6 million-hectare) site the government's Indian Foundation identified in 1993 as belonging to the Makuxi, Wapixana, Ingariko, Tauperang and Patamona tribes.

They also warned that conflict between Indians and wildcat miners who live in the towns would continue. "This decision was eminently political," the Indian Council of Roraima said in a statement. It said the ruling sought to win support from local politicians for President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's upcoming bid to rewrite the constitution and run for re-election.

"(The ruling) is based on shaky legal concepts that do not hide the political nature of this decision," the Instituto Socioambiental, a Sao Paulo-based group said in a statement. "It is a Trojan Horse for the rights of the 11,000 Indians of five ethnic groups who traditionally live in Raposa/Serra do Sol."

Schwartzman said the ruling set a "disastrous precedent" for nearly 200 other Indian reservations in the process of being demarcated. "It's an invitation to conflict and, potentially, to violence," he said.
Milton Seligman, the Justice Ministry's executive secretary, denied there would be any reduction in the size of Raposa/Serra do Sol. He also denied political motives were behind the ruling.
